creator: dr.truitt_sandiego
title: Mohs surgery isn’t just about clearing the visible tumor — it’s about knowing when to look deeper. 🩺
caption:
Mohs surgery isn’t just about clearing the visible tumor — it’s about knowing when to look deeper. 🩺

In this case, my patient had an aggressive squamous cell carcinoma, and even after the Mohs slides were clear, experience told me to take one more step. By sending the tissue for additional pathology and immunostaining, we confirmed there was no perineural involvement — a rare but serious pattern where skin cancer can travel along nerves.

That’s why attention to detail matters in Mohs micrograp
transcript: So, I recently had a really interesting Mohs case. So, Mohs is micrographic surgery to help clear tumors of the skin. Particularly, usually it's basal cell or squamous cell skin cancers. So, this particular patient had a squamous cell skin cancer. And just because you're necessarily clear on the Mohs slides, which is what normally would happen, sometimes that's not always the case. And I think this is where experience comes into play. So, I've been doing Mohs for a few years. And what I found is that if I see a really aggressive tumor on the first stage of Mohs, I keep going until it's clear. But then what I do is package everything up and send it off to my um pathologist. And then they will special stain it and go through the remainder of the block. I know this gets a little bit technical, but what they do is look at the remainder of the center tissue to see if potentially there's any perineural involvement. Perineural involvement means that the skin cancer has actually started to wrap around nerves. And it what happens is that it can actually skip down the nerve. So, you may have a clear margin with Mohs, but the skin cancer may have skipped down. Now, this is very rare. So, this is really more with just aggressive tumors. And you can see that morphology on the slides when you're looking at it. And you kind of have maybe a guess or a hunch that this is a really an aggressive tumor. I should have my pathologist actually immunostain specifically to look at the nerves. So, one thing to think about.

current.subject: when clear mohs margins aren't enough
current.claim: For aggressive squamous cell cancers, extra pathology after clear Mohs margins can rule out perineural spread.

Boils develop when bacteria infect a **hair follicle** or nearby oil gland. Your immune system responds by sending white blood cells to fight the infection, leading to a buildup of pus.

⚠️ As pressure increases, the area becomes red, swollen, warm, and painful.

💡 Most boils heal with proper treatment, but large, recurrent, or spreading boils should be evaluated by a healthcare professional.

But as they die along with bacteria and damaged tissue, a thick pocket of pus begins to form beneath the skin. As more pus builds up, stretches the skin, causing pain and swelling. Eventually, the boil drains, releasing the trapped pus and allowing the infection to begin healing.

It's called Mohs micrographic excision. And it's a technique developed by Doctor Frederick Mohs, I believe it's back in the 50s at the university of Wisconsin. Anyway, it's, um, it's a real time analysis of the tumor as it comes off in three dimensions. So it's not only going around the, uh, skin cancer in question, it's going under it. And then with each what's called layer being removed, it's immediately evaluated by the most surgeon who is trained dermatopathologist or a skin, uh, pathologist. And so they look at it right underneath the microscope right then and there, and they continue to go down. You can see here that only this little yellow spot is the remaining tumor. So they go to here, they get most of it out, but they see just a little bit is still left. So then over here, they just focus on that one area. So with this three dimensional tumor mapping, they have a very high degree of clearance, a relatively low degree of collateral damage, and a very low degree of recurrent disease. So it's actually the gold standard for basal cell and squamous cell carcinoma of the head and neck, the area in which I specialize for reconstruction. It also can be used in some forms of melanoma for a specially trained Amount of pathologist. And then what I do is I many times will come in and help to reconstruct the defect or the hole that is left over. So there's the difference. And just kind of a little factoids about that.
